query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Reducing carbon content in an iron-based alloy (i.e., using low-carbon steel) increases ductility due to fewer carbide formations and enhanced dislocation mobility.
generation.material_initial_state: Iron-carbon alloy with conventional medium carbon levels (~0.3–0.6 wt% C).
generation.intervention: Lower the carbon content to below ~0.10 wt% while maintaining similar processing conditions.
generation.conditions: Perform standard tensile tests at room temperature on both low-carbon steel and medium-carbon steel samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced carbide formation in the matrix, enabling dislocations to move more freely.
generation.mechanism: By lowering the amount of carbon, there are fewer carbon atoms to form precipitates, thereby reducing obstacles to slip and enhancing ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable increase in elongation (for example, an increase in total elongation by several percentage points) compared to the medium-carbon steel baseline, indicating improved ductility.
generation.baseline: Medium-carbon steel samples (~0.3–0.6 wt% C) tested under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: Excessively low carbon contents (e.g., approaching ultra-low-carbon steels) or additional alloying elements and heat treatments may alter or overshadow the effect, limiting generalizability.
generation.uncertainty: No direct measurement data provided here, so the specific improvement in elongation is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare sets of steel samples with varying carbon contents (e.g., 0.05, 0.10, 0.30, and 0.60 wt%). Conduct consistent tensile tests on each set.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) to quantify carbide formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If reducing carbon content below 0.10 wt% does not improve elongation relative to medium-carbon steel under identical processing conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.
